title: Cell Phones and Driving
osha_standards: OSH Act Section 5(a)(1) General Duty Clause
summary: Distracted driving is any time your eyes leave the road, your hands leave the wheel, or your mind leaves driving. Hands-free phones are just as distracting as handheld ones.
talking_points: Do not use your phone while driving. Pull over in a safe location to look up directions, text, or make or receive a call.
There are three kinds of distraction: visual (eyes off the road), manual (hands off the wheel), and cognitive (mind off driving).
Hands-free phones are just as distracting as handheld phones. Your brain has limited capacity for attention.
Drivers who use cell phones may look at but fail to see up to 50% of the information in their driving environment.
Make adjustments to your vehicle, such as controls and directions, before you drive.
Do not reach for items on the floor, open the glove box, or try to catch falling objects while driving.
Avoid emotional conversations with passengers, or pull over safely to continue them.
Focus on the vehicles, pedestrians, cyclists, and objects around you that may mean you need to act fast.
site_hazards_to_check: Phones, tablets, or GPS units mounted or held where the driver must look away or reach
Loose items on the floor or seat that could slide or fall while driving
Directions or radio not set before the vehicle moves
Company vehicles without a clear no-phone-use policy communicated to drivers
discussion_questions: Which of the three distraction types (visual, manual, cognitive) do you face most when driving for work?
Why is a hands-free call still a risk?
Where can we safely pull over to make or take a call on our route today?
